title: Assessing exogenous carbohydrate intake needed to optimize human endurance performance across sex: insights from modeling runners pursuing a sub-2-h marathon
authors: Lukasiewicz CJ, Vandiver KJ, Albert ED, Kirby BS, Jacobs RA
population: Modelled elite runners (120 male, 120 female) attempting a sub-2-h marathon, parameterised from published literature
findings: Modelled exogenous CHO needed was 93 +/- 26 g/h (males) and 108 +/- 22 g/h (females) (P < 0.0001, d = 0.61).
Without exogenous CHO, males depleted glycogen in 84 +/- 7 min vs 71 +/- 5 min for females.
Intakes <= 90 g/h were insufficient for 65% of modelled runners; sufficient for 56 of 120 males and 28 of 120 females.
Authors say research on benefits of > 90 g/h should prioritise female athlete inclusion.
limitations: Pure simulation of an elite two-hour marathon at very high intensity; not ultra, not recreational; assumptions on glycogen stores and oxidation; no empirical validation.
implications: Evidence for sex-specific CHO targets is open: do not apply sex multipliers to ultra paces.
No change to the low-intensity 100-mile pathway; use only as a flag that high-CHO evidence is male-dominated.

verification.notes: Crossref match; modelling numbers from Europe PMC abstract.
